headline: Sussex kelp restoration enters its fifth winter with the first signs of a self-sustaining bed
standfirst: Trawling was excluded from 300 square kilometres in 2021. The kelp took three years to show up, and is now reproducing without help.

image.alt: Kelp fronds photographed from below in green water

body.text: When the byelaw came into force, the seabed off Sussex was mostly bare. Five winters later, divers are recording continuous kelp canopy across sections of ground that had held nothing but scoured gravel since the 1980s.
The significant change this year is not the extent. It is that the bed is now producing its own spores in sufficient density to colonise new ground without seeding.
You stop counting plants and start counting square metres. That is the moment it becomes a habitat rather than a project.

Cuttlefish and bass have returned in numbers that local charter skippers describe as unrecognisable from a decade ago. The commercial question — whether the closure eventually pays for itself in improved catches outside the boundary — remains open.
